name: Agathon of Alexandria
knownFor: Coptic patriarch of Alexandria after Benjamin I. Under Heraclius he served Benjamin's hidden flock disguised as a carpenter. As patriarch he freed captives from Sicily and hid from a Chalcedonian governor.
dates: B. Evetts heads his life in the History of the Patriarchs 661 to 677. The History says he sat seventeen years and died on the 16th of the Coptic month Babah. René Basset's French of the Arabic Synaxarium brackets 659 to 667. A note in Evetts's 1895 English of Abu Salih gives 658 to 677, with a question mark
place: Alexandria. A native of Mareotis, the History says
role: Patriarch of Alexandria, the thirty-ninth in the History's count

keyWorks.title: Account of the consecration of the church of Saint Macarius
keyWorks.about: told in his voice inside the History's life of Benjamin I. Benjamin's vision and his rules for the church come through it. Eusèbe Renaudot called it a fable under Agathon's name

traces: A vision named John of Samannud to him as his successor, the History says. Some asked Agathon to make John a bishop of Upper Egypt, but God was keeping him for the throne.
The History dates a church dedicated to Saint Macarius to his days, without saying who built it. The brothers grew so many that they built cells near the Marsh.
He ordained Simon I of Alexandria, the later patriarch, a priest, says the History's life of Simon.
remembered: The Arabic Synaxarium, the Coptic church's book of saints' days, keeps him on the 16th of Babah in René Basset's French. It adds that he was bound when he was made patriarch.
The Ethiopic Synaxarium, in E. A. Wallis Budge's English, keeps him on the 16th of Tekemt. It says he died of overwork, after nineteen years.

A book on the churches of Egypt, under the name of Abu Salih, tells a story of him at al-Ushmunain. A woodcutter, sent by the governor, struck a tree the patriarch stood under. The axe flew back into the woodcutter's face.

uncertain: His life rests on the History of the Patriarchs, a later Arabic history of the Coptic church. It does not name the writer of his life.

The account told in his voice in Benjamin's life. Eusèbe Renaudot, a Catholic scholar writing in 1713, calls the Coptic patriarchs heretics. He calls the account a fable under Agathon's name, and judges Benjamin's canons in it the work of later Copts.

His years. The History and the Arabic Synaxarium give seventeen. The Ethiopic Synaxarium gives nineteen, and so does Renaudot's reading of the History. Renaudot reports sixteen from the historian Makrizi.
The governor's name. The History's text has Theodore, and B. Evetts notes that some manuscripts have Theodosius. Both synaxaria have Theodosius.
The fleet. The History says Theodore's demands cost him seven thousand denarii. Basset's synaxarium has seven thousand dinars a year, and Budge's seven hundred.
The captives. The History adds that those he freed were Gaianites and Barsanuphians, sects outside his church.
His consecration. Both synaxaria say he was bound when he was made patriarch. The History does not say so.
